title: How the oil capital of the US welcomed a solar power boom
text:
Steve Cargil's family has farmed the flat, dry land around Uvalde, a small city in southwest Texas, since 1953.

Cargil, 67, had always assumed that one of his three children would eventually take it over, the way he had from his father.

But that assumption took a hit one night in 2018 after a violent hailstorm.

Cargil and his son, Ryan, had spent months nursing crops of cabbage and onions to harvest. Then a storm rolled through and destroyed them overnight.

"I remember my son saying, 'Dad, I just don't know if I can do this. You do everything right, and we work so hard, and you come out one morning and it's all gone'," Cargil says.

Cargil's farm was at risk of ending with him, he says, with none of his three children wanting to farm full time. For years, that left him wondering what would happen to the land, and to his own retirement, since farmers rarely have a pension to fall back on.

Then in 2001 Cargil signed a deal to lease 600 acres of his land, about a quarter of the total, to a company called OCI Energy which built a vast solar farm.

"Never in my wildest dreams did I think that a solar project would be on my farm," Cargil says. Looking back now, he calls it a blessing.

The lease, which pays Cargil $200,000 (£150,000) a year, has let him keep his farm running through a punishing drought. He has been able to concentrate his water irrigation allowance on the land he still farms, and he has stopped losing sleep over rises in the price of things such as diesel and fertiliser. "It's changed my life."

Texas, which remains the largest oil producer in the US, earlier this year overtook California to become the country's biggest generator of electricity from solar farms. , external

And in March of last year, more electricity was produced by solar in Texas than from coal for the first time, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

On hot afternoons, when demand for power peaks, solar is now regularly supplying around a third of the electricity used across Texas, says Mark Stover, executive director of the Texas Solar and Storage Association.

He says that the solar boom is being driven by two main things. Firstly, it is cheap and quick to connect solar farms to Texas' power grid, which is separate to the rest of the US. Secondly, Texas has a huge and growing appetite for electricity, driven by a burgeoning population.

Between 2015 and 2025, Texas's population increased by 15.8%, , external making it one of the fastest-growing states in the nation.

"We need a whole lot of power in Texas, and we need it quickly," Stover says.

Solar has also become inexpensive. James Scott, vice president of project development at OCI, says the technology has had years of small manufacturing gains that brought the price down to the point where it is now the cheapest way to generate power in the state.

"No one would have believed that 20 years ago," Scott says.

Once a project is built, he says, the price of the electricity it produces can be fixed for decades, since the fuel, sunlight, is free.

"We'll charge you $40 a megawatt hour for the next 25 years," Scott says, adding that large buyers such as Amazon and Apple value being able to lock in a price for that long.

By contrast, new coal plants in the US produce power at nearly $90 megawatts per hour, says the Energy Information Administration.

Farmers have become central to that growth because solar developers need large stretches of flat land.

Stover says the industry is now paying out multigenerational income to families through leases that typically run 25 to 30 years and rise in value each year, letting some retire, set up family trusts, or simply keep a farm solvent.

Stover argues solar's footprint is smaller than critics assume. "The industry is utilizing less than 0.15% of Texas land," he says.

Yet solar has its opponents. In Franklin County, in northeast Texas, a small group of residents has spent the past few years fighting its growth.

BF Hicks, a local lawyer whose family has owned land in the county since the 1800s, says he watched neighbours sign 30-year leases with solar companies and bulldozers clear centuries-old oak trees near his property.

He describes a summer when smoke from burning cleared land hung over his town for weeks. "It got real personal," he says, when a solar farm was built next to his family's cemetery. His relatives have been buried here dating back two centuries.

David Truesdale, a retired federal law enforcement agent who moved to the county to get away from city life, says he became involved after learning that a neighbouring solar project would sit near his home. And that under Texan law no environmental review was required.

"We're destroying the world as we're trying to save it," Truesdale says of the land clearing he has seen. He also points to the large lithium-ion battery units installed alongside many solar farms, drawing a comparison to fires that have occasionally engulfed similar batteries in electric bikes.

"If one of those things catches fire, they go off in series, so each one will progressively cause another one to go off," he says.

Both men say their objections are not about politics. Franklin County is solidly conservative, but its residents helped push through one of the state's first county-level moratoriums on new solar construction, before it was later rescinded under legal pressure from developers.

Their complaints echo a broader unease that has followed solar's expansion into rural Texas - worries about visual impact, water runoff after land is cleared, and battery storage units that scorch their land.

President Trump has called solar and wind power "farmer destroying" and moved to unwind tax credits for renewable projects.…

title: When Bellamy watched on as Ronaldo caused lockdown
text:
With five Ballon d'Or wins, eight league titles, five Champions Leagues, a European Championship and a pair of Nations League triumphs among his glut of honours, Cristiano Ronaldo's status as one of football's all-time greats is not in doubt.

But a chance encounter with the Portugal legend helped Wales boss Craig Bellamy appreciate that the 41-year-old is significantly more than just a footballing icon.

Bellamy was on a pre-season trip to Lisbon during his time as an assistant to manager Vincent Kompany at Burnley when the Portuguese capital's airport was effectively put into lockdown.

It led to the Welshman describing Ronaldo as "beyond a superstar" after he realised the vast presence of police and security officials were to help escort the global icon.

"So we got to the airport and the police were everywhere. It was on lockdown," Bellamy said.

Ronaldo spurred on by 1,000 goals and Portugal glory

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

"We're Burnley and we had a little bit of VIP. We were on a coach, we were chartered but still had to go into the airport a certain way.

"It was like rows of police with police cars everywhere. We thought, 'something has happened, there must be a warning here'.

"Everything was locked off. People in the terminal, you name it. We couldn't get off the coach and we had to wait for what we thought was a security breach or something.

"We are stuck on the coach for 10, 15 minutes and suddenly this car turns up, it parks and a guy walks out, goes in the boot, grabs a rucksack and someone else gets out and puts the rucksack on and who is it? Ronaldo."

Bellamy added: "He is walking on his own with police everywhere and Lisbon airport locked off. Even the police were taking pictures. No-one could bother him.

"It was the coolest walk I have ever watched for a minute.

"We were all on the coach and our jaws dropped. Everyone who had been moaning quickly shut up. It was like presidents stuff."

Bellamy last shared a pitch with Ronaldo in October 2008 as the Portuguese scored twice for Manchester United in a 2-0 Premier League win over West Ham United at Old Trafford.

He is now set to manage his country against the 233-cap international as Wales kick-start their Nations League A campaign in Portugal on Thursday night.

As he bids to conjure up a plan to nullify Ronaldo and the rest of the star-studded Portugal squad at the Estadio Jose Alvalade, Bellamy was eager to fully reflect on the experience of the forward he witnessed at Lisbon airport.

"How can you lock off a whole airport?" added Bellamy.

"I would not be able to get my computer through customs in Cardiff airport. What have I just seen?

"The reason I'm telling the story is because that's how big this guy is.

"It was like, 'wow'. I'm so glad I saw that moment because he is beyond a superstar."

What will 'greatest captain' bring to Bellamy's Wales?

FAW chief questions Infantino's Fifa reform claims

During the summer, Ronaldo confirmed the 2026 World Cup would be his last.

However, the Al-Nassr frontman has so far not revealed when he will finally bring his glittering career to an end.

Despite the uncertainty surrounding Ronaldo's future, Bellamy says he can fully understand why the forward - now in his 24th year as a senior Portugal international - is still operating at an elite level.

"I'm not surprised he is still playing with the professionalism he has shown," added Bellamy.

"It's also how clever he is, he knows how to protect himself, he knows not to waste his energy at certain times and he's still got the habit of goal-scoring, and you never lose that.

"We're talking about not just one of the greatest players of our generation, we're talking all generations with what he has been able to do. He's beyond a superstar."

Inside the Wales camp: Jordan James & Connor Roberts

For all of the spotlight on Ronaldo and his team-mates, Bellamy knows his full focus - along with that of his players and staff - must be on how Wales can leave the City of Light with a positive result.

The head coach's already tough task has been made harder by the fact he will be without players including Harry Wilson, Joe Rodon, Karl Darlow, Nathan Broadhead, Dylan Lawlor, Rubin Colwill and Isaak Davies in Lisbon.

But Bellamy has urged his players to show the right kind of fight as they bid to upset the odds and remain in the top tier of the Nations League over the coming months.

"We have to be excited, but not too excited," he added.

"We have worked hard to get into League A, so what can we do to stay in it? If we do then it will help us massively and that's the motivation.

"You want to be in these moments. I'm telling you, when your playing days finish, you won't remember Bury away and all that. These moments you will remember and will live with you.

"But you also want to remember how you performed. You don't want this to get too much.

"I want my players to go out and give everything. They should love every second of it. That's the drive for this."

title: The moment Antonelli knew he had been transformed as an F1 driver
text:
Kimi Antonelli says he knew from the first moment he drove this year's Mercedes that he would be transformed as a Formula 1 driver in 2026.

The 20-year-old Italian, who is running away with the world championship in only his second season in F1, is reflecting on his breakthrough year in the sport in an exclusive interview with BBC Sport.

A difficult debut season last year had left external expectations of Antonelli low at the start of 2026. But on a typically damp and cold January day at Silverstone, he already sensed that something special might be on the cards.

"It was just a few laps in the wet," Antonelli says, "but I just felt better in the car, much better than I felt last year. Also the car felt well, but I just felt better mentally in the car. Less tense, more relaxed and more mature."

Last year, he says, was "not great". "I was driving very tense most of the time, I wasn't able to extract the potential out of me," he says.

"This year, it's a lot different. The mindset has been the biggest change."

Fast forward eight months and the effects of that new headspace are plain to see.

After 14 grands prix, and with either eight or nine remaining depending on the war in the Middle East, Antonelli is a massive 81 points clear of team-mate George Russell.

Not only that, but he looks so in control. Always fast, always composed, a factor in every grand prix. Everyone knows the championship is basically over, barring some kind of dramatic misfortune.

Even then, Antonelli says he is "still finding my way" in F1.

The journey Antonelli has been on in the past two years is remarkable, and he says even he is "surprised" by the extent of his progress this year.

He was comprehensively outperformed by Russell in 2025. So when it was obvious that Mercedes would start the new regulatory era with an advantage, it was the Briton who started the season as championship favourite.

Russell duly won the opening race in Australia, but Antonelli was less than three seconds behind him at the flag. This, he says, was the second moment of realisation of what might be possible.

"I had a big, big crash in FP3," Antonelli recalls. "But then thanks to the mechanics - who all throughout the season have done an incredible job, but on that specific occasion, it is a miracle - I was able to go back in the car and push again in the high speed and getting close to the limit.

"The crash, definitely it compromised a little bit qualifying and the race because we couldn't set up properly the car. I mean, the car was still very quick. But it was not easy.

"Still being able to stay close despite that, I was like, 'OK, you know, it's not going to be a walk in the park. It's going to be very tough', but I knew already that it was a different story compared to last year.

"If it would have happened last year, I wouldn't have been able to overcome that."

Antonelli's first season in F1 was haunted by an incident that happened the first time he drove on a grand prix weekend.

At the 2024 Italian Grand Prix, the day before they formally announced Antonelli was the replacement for Ferrari-bound Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes gave him an outing in first practice at Monza.

He was blindingly fast on his first flying lap - but then crashed heavily on his second.

Team principal Toto Wolff played it down at the time, saying he was well aware there would be mistakes from Antonelli as he found his feet in F1. But behind the scenes the incident had had a big impact on the young man.

"Monza stayed in my head for a very long time," Antonelli says. "I think all throughout last season, at least. Definitely that was a big thing that was kind of slowing me down.

"This memory of being afraid to do a mistake, also because going through the difficult period (in the middle of 2025), this memory was even stronger in my head, if you know what I mean.

"Because it was already a difficult period and I was like, 'If I even do a mistake or I crash, it's even worse.'

"So yeah, it's been a thing that has been bothering me a lot last year. This year I was able to just put it behind."

Doing so has involved a lot of work behind the scenes, analysing what happened in 2025, understanding what had gone well, what had not, and why, and what he could do to improve.

"The mindset going into this season, it was mainly trying to be able to extract more out of my potential," Antonelli says. "Trying to, first of all, do a better job than previous year. But as well trying to put things more together.

"The preparation that I did in pre-season was very, very intense. But it helped me a lot to arrive ready for this season.

"Plus, I did a lot of work with my mental coach. Trying to get my head right, my thoughts right on understanding the goal, and understanding that the most important thing is to be ready and to stay present in the moment.

"Not trying to think about final results or what would happen if I wouldn't achieve that. But just trying to be present and trying to do the best with what you can do in the moment."

Still, though, he admits to be "definitely surprised" at how much progress he has made.

"I knew that I was going to be better than my first year," he says. "Obviously, because I think last year, towards the end of the season, I started to put things more together, starting to extract more performance. But still, it was still not great.

"Whereas this year, it's a lot different. Also as well, with the first win, the first pole, it took a lot of weight off my shoulder."

Antonelli has blossomed. Everything seems to be coming so easily to him. If he drops back in a race, he recovers seamlessly and quickly. Overtaking moves are done quickly and decisively. There's not been a circuit on which he has lacked pace.

Russell, by contrast, has admitted to struggling and - while not trying to take anything away from Antonelli, who he is always quick to praise - has expressed his opinion that his his driving style does not suit this year's new cars.…

title: Man Utd still £1bn in debt with £63.5m spent on new stadium
text:
Manchester United's overall debt remains over £1bn despite Sir Jim Ratcliffe's extensive cost-cutting measures, with the club also confirming it has spent £63.5m buying land for the team's new stadium.

Amid a backdrop of fan protests and a disappointing start to the season that has left United 12th in the Premier League and already out of the EFL Cup, the club have announced record revenues of £677.6m and a £22.6m operating profit despite not playing in Europe for the first time in a decade.

This represents a huge shift from the £113.2m loss in 2023-24.

However, while United have saved £8.5m of a projected £16.5m pay-off to axed boss Ruben Amorim after he accepted a job at AC Milan, other costs have increased.

Net finance costs for the year were £69.6m, an increase of 228.3%. United put most of this down to a foreign exchange loss. According to football finance expert Kieran Maguire, net finance costs alone have now exceeded £1bn since the leveraged Glazer family buyout in 2005.

In addition, United also confirmed they spent £63.5m of an additional $125m (£94.14m) added to their historic debt during a summer refinancing move on land for their new stadium. The club have not explained what they have done with the remainder. The stadium itself is likely to cost in excess of £2bn.

It means the club's overall debt, while reducing from £1.3bn at the end of December, is still over £1bn, made up of the historic debt, which now stands at £577.6m, the £111.4m outstanding on its revolving credit facility, and outstanding transfer fees, which club sources say represents approximately 75% of the £473m listed and being owed as 'trade and other payables'.

This comes at a time when supporters are furious about what they believe to be chronic under investment in Michael Carrick's first-team squad this summer.

United spent £148m on three new signings - Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans. It was less than a third of the £458m Manchester City invested in their squad and lower even than promoted Ipswich.

However, fans are angry there was no additional left-back purchased to provide competition for Luke Shaw, who has missed three matches because of injury already, or striking support for Benjamin Sesko, who missed pre-season as he recovered from a shin complaint that has already resurfaced.

While United argue the additional funds were earmarked for their stadium, to be built 350 yards away from where Old Trafford stands, the loan itself is lodged within club accounts.

"We are pleased to have secured record revenues," said chief executive Omar Berrada.

"This demonstrates the underlying strength of our business, and shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years.

"While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable.

"With that financial sustainability in mind, we have strengthened both our men's and women's teams during the summer window and our men's team has seen the return of Champions League football to Old Trafford."

United have also been criticised for a lack of investment in the Women's Super League squad, who currently sit second bottom of the table with one point from three games.

Ratcliffe previously argued the club had to take strong action to slash losses. Two lots of redundancies led to 450 people losing their jobs, while United have confirmed their latest set of salary costs have reduced by £11.3m to £302m.

"This is primarily due to changes in the make-up of the men's first-team squad, combined with savings associated with headcount reduction programs implemented over the previous two fiscal years," said the club.

title: Manchester United report seventh straight annual loss and sell fans £125 grass clumps
author: Matt Hughes
text:
Net loss of £43m for year ended 30 June 2026

Revenue hits record £677.6m and forecast to grow

Manchester United have reported an annual loss for the seventh ­successive year, taking the club’s combined losses to £444m since 2019.

The financial results were released as it emerged United are raising revenue by selling small clumps of grass from the Old Trafford pitch to supporters. United relaid the playing surface for the first time in 14 years this summer , and an email to fans has offered them the chance to buy 7cm x 7cm clumps of turf for £125.

The £43m net loss for 2025-26 is a significant increase on the £33m for the previous 12 months, with compensation paid to the sacked manager Ruben Amorim a contributory factor along with the decision to increase the club’s borrowing facility by £93m to help fund the redevelopment of Old Trafford.

United’s continued losses come despite record revenue of £677.6m – up 1.7% on the previous 12 months – and the implementation of a major cost-cutting regime by Sir Jim Ratcliffe under which hundreds of staff have lost their jobs.

In discussing United’s results on an investor call, the chief executive, Omar Berrada, said the club’s summer transfer window, during which they spent £155m on three players, had been planned with “financial sustainability in mind” in an indication that the budget will continue to be tight for new manager, Michael Carrick.

That is underlined by the fact that United’s wage bill dropped to £301m, down 3.6% on the previous year, more than £100m lower than Manchester City’s.

While United reported operating profits of £22.6m for the 12 months to 30 June 2026 the increase in revenue was more than offset by the cost of financing the club. Net finance costs more than tripled to £69.2m from £21.2m in the previous year, partly owing to foreign-exchange ­movements, and the club refinanced several loans, increasing their net debt from £471.9m to £577.6m.

United sources have said the refinancing provided funding for the £63.5m purchase of a plot of land next to Old Trafford required to build their proposed new 100,000 capacity stadium, the first major investment in a complex project that could end up costing more than £2bn.

Berrada said the results demonstrated “the underlying strength of our business, particularly in a season without European football” and said: “This shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years. It also proves Manchester United’s enduring popularity and commercial strength. While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable.”

United are confident their financial outlook will improve over the next 12 months owing to the club’s return to the Champions League and the start of increased sponsorship deals with the training-kit partner Betway and shirt-sleeve partner SumUp, which will bring in £20m and £22m a year respectively. The club is forecasting revenue of between £740m and £760m for 2026-27.

title: Slip sliding away: football season-ticket holders fear falling down pecking order
author: Paul MacInnes
text:
It is a symbol of the connection between the fanbase and club, but there is a growing fear executives would prefer stadiums full of one-off tourists

T he document known as “the oldest football season ticket in the world” promises its bearer access to every Burnley home game of the 1884-85 season. It is a ticket that predates the Football League by four years, with all the fixtures played against east Lancashire neighbours. All the same, the legend on the ticket carries a stern warning: “This card is not transferable. Any member violating this rule will be at once expelled from the club.”

For Burnley 1884 read Manchester United 2026. While the oldest remaining season ticket is preserved safely at Turf Moor, at Old Trafford 685 season tickets were voided this summer after a club investigation found evidence of their having been resold on the secondary market. United said such practices “undermine fair access to tickets for genuine supporters and have no place at Manchester United”. United fan groups again protested against the actions of the club’s ownership, claiming: “The way you treat us is a disgrace.”

Nearly 150 years after fans started paying up front to watch their team, the season ticket remains a key component in the success of English football. It is also an enduring source of conflict between supporters and clubs, with tensions seemingly reaching new heights.

Arsenal, like United, have continued to act against the perceived misuse of tickets, suspending nearly 74,000 club accounts since they began a crackdown in 2024. This summer Chelsea became the latest club to insist on minimum levels of attendance to retain your ticket for the following season. Bournemouth moved 600 season-ticket holders to accommodate new hospitality seats and 14 out of the 20 top-flight sides raised their season-ticket prices.

Season-ticket holders have long felt undervalued. But there is a growing sense, especially among fans of the biggest clubs, that they are falling ever further down the pecking order as economic imperatives change. It is a feeling that intensified after a World Cup that seemed precision-tooled to extract as much money as possible from the most devoted fans. One Liverpool supporter crystallised common fears when he appeared on The Overlap at the start of the season arguing that a big club would soon try to get rid of season tickets altogether. The clip went viral.

The Football Supporters’ Association argues that clubs’ present behaviour shows an antagonism towards season-ticket holders. “There’s a sense from supporter groups at the most successful teams that their club executives and owners don’t fully appreciate season ticket holders and would rather have stadiums full of one-off visitors,” an FSA spokesperson said.

“Those who only measure things by the bottom line see season-ticket holders as a group whose matchday spend is lower than the once-a-year fan who will fill their bag at the club shop and pay a bigger premium for their ticket. It’s a shortsighted vision.”

The claim that clubs want to swap longstanding supporters for one-off tourists is at the heart of many fans’ fears over season tickets and, to a certain extent, it bears out. Dominik Schreyer, a professor of sports economics at the WHU Otto Beisheim School of Management in Düsseldorf, says season tickets “come at a cost” for clubs.

“In the Premier League , demand is way higher than seat supply,” Schreyer says. “But season-ticket holders get discounted seats, right? They are also more likely to be no-shows. When they do come they spend less on food, less on merchandise and they come later to the stadium. They also don’t churn, because these tickets are so scarce that nobody in their right mind would give them away. Every year the average age grows by one because there is no one new getting tickets. So for the clubs, there are a lot of economic problems from their season-ticket holders.”

That, however, is only one side of the ledger. “What we should not forget is that, in the end, season‑ticket holders are part of a product that, in the case of the Premier League, is marketed to a global audience,” Schreyer says.

“They are creating an atmosphere. Season-ticket holders are also used to all the rules and the rituals and the songs, the moments that make this experience very special. So tourists want to come because they want to experience it. If you were to get rid of all the season-ticket holders, you would have all the operational and coordination costs of doing it and the product would not be the same any more.”

There are other reasons why season tickets work for clubs, not least because they generate a largely predictable amount of revenue that turns up at the same time each year (at the very end of the season where it can be usefully deployed to help with transfer spending limits).

For most clubs, it would not be feasible to replace season‑ticket holders with one-off fans even if they wanted to. But with the average number of season tickets at any given Premier League fixture running at 75% of all tickets, is there a case that this number should not be set in stone? Could access to matches be broadened without killing off a part of what made them great?

“In theory, you could give all the seats to season-ticket holders and still have a lot of tickets for new fans if you manage it effectively,” Schreyer says. “You just need to change the mechanism in order to get the ticket that is unused on to the secondary market.”…

text: Manchester United fan Jay Motty reflects on a 'disastrous' start to the season for his club and why he's worried about Marcus Rashford's form
